origin.description: Asymmetry coefficient for an empirical Lorenz curve, as proposed for comparing inequality alongside the Gini coefficient.
origin.usage: Lasym(x, n = rep(1, length(x)), interval = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE)

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: Numeric vector. Entries are expected to be non-negative.

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Frequencies, one per entry of x. The default is a vector of ones as long as x.

arguments.name: interval
arguments.text: If observations land exactly on the mean, TRUE returns the two endpoint asymmetry coefficients and FALSE returns their midpoint.

arguments.name: na.rm
arguments.text: If TRUE, missing values are removed before the coefficient is computed. If FALSE, any missing x yields NA.

origin.details: Damgaard and Weiner proposed this coefficient as a companion to the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient when comparing inequality, in particular for plant size or fecundity. It locates the asymmetry of the Lorenz curve rather than only its distance from equality.
origin.value: A single coefficient, or two coefficients when interval is TRUE and some observations equal the mean.
origin.example:
## Examples from Damgaard & Weiner (2000)

## Figure 2
x <- rep(c(50/9, 50), c(9, 1))
y <- rep(c(2, 18), c(5, 5))
plot(table(x))
plot(table(y))

## statistics
mean(x)
mean(y)
Gini(x, corr = TRUE)
Gini(y, corr = TRUE)
Lasym(x)
Lasym(y)

## Figure 3
plot(Lc(x))
lines(Lc(y), col = "slategray")
abline(1, -1, lty = 2)

translation.description: Asymmetry coefficient for an empirical Lorenz curve, as proposed for comparing inequality alongside the Gini coefficient.

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: One-dimensional numeric sample. Entries are expected to be non-negative.

arguments.name: n
arguments.text: Frequencies. None builds a one for every original entry of x, before missing values are removed.

arguments.name: interval
arguments.text: When some observations equal the weighted mean, true returns both endpoint coefficients and false returns their average.

arguments.name: na_rm
arguments.text: This is na.rm in R. If true, missing x values are removed first. If false, any missing x returns a length-1 NaN array, or a length-2 NaN array when interval is true.

translation.details: The coefficient follows Damgaard and Weiner: sort the sample, take the weighted mean as the sum of weight times value over the sum of the weights, and combine the mass and the total sitting below that mean. If nothing equals the mean, the share is interpolated between the observations on either side. If some do, the two conventional endpoints are averaged unless an interval was requested.
translation.value: A one-dimensional NumPy array of length 1, or of length 2 when an interval of coefficients is requested and some observations equal the mean.
translation.example:
import numpy as np
from ineq.lorenz import Lasym

x = np.repeat([50 / 9, 50], [9, 1])
y = np.repeat([2, 18], [5, 5])
print(Lasym(x))
print(Lasym(y))
